|---|---|
| commission receivable prepaid | 1 200 |
| insurance accrued | 650 |

What was the correct amount of the retained earnings?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The amount charged to the income statement for an income or an expense should be the amount that was due for the financial period

  - This is not necessarily the amount that was paid or received
- Subtract the \$1 200 prepaid commission from the income amount on the income statement

  - This is because this amount relates to the next financial period, not the current one
  - Therefore the income decreases by \$1 200
- Add the \$650 accrued insurance to the expense amount on the income statement

  - This is because this amount relates to the current financial year and should be included even though it has not yet been paid
  - Therefore the expenses increase by \$650
- Retained earnings increase if the profit increases and decrease if the profit decreases
- Profit = gross profit + other income - expenses

  - If the income decreases by \$1 200 then the profit decreases by \$1 200
  - If the expenses increase by \$650 then the profit decreases by \$650
- Correct retained earnings = \$42 540 - \$1 200 - \$650 = \$40 690

**B** is incorrect; you get this answer if you incorrectly treat the accrued insurance as prepaid insurance or as an accrued income

**C** is incorrect; you get this answer if you incorrectly treat the prepaid commission as an accrued commission or as a prepaid expense

**D** is incorrect; you get this answer if you incorrectly add both amounts to the retained earnings

parts.problemMd:
A manufacturing company provided the following information.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| cost of raw materials | 162 000 |
| factory rent | 31 000 |
| direct wages | 83 000 |
| factory supervisor's salary | 28 000 |
| depreciation of machinery | 35 000 |
| machinery repairs | 10 000 |

What was the prime cost of manufacturing?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The prime cost is the total of the direct costs

  - direct materials, direct labour and direct expenses
- Determine whether each cost is direct or indirect

  - raw materials is a direct cost
  - factory rent is an indirect cost
  - direct wages are a direct cost
  - factory supervisor's salary is an indirect cost
  - depreciation of machinery is an indirect cost
  - machinery repairs are an indirect cost
- Add together the direct costs

  - \$162 000 + \$83 000 = \$245 000

**A** is incorrect; it is missing the direct wages

**C** is incorrect; this has incorrectly included the factory supervisor's salary (the factory supervisor is not directly linked to the production of the goods)

**D** is incorrect; this is the total of all the direct and indirect costs

parts.problemMd:
A manufacturing business started on 1 May 2023.  The owner provided the following information about the first year in business.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| prime cost | 65 420 |
| factory overheads | 17 270 |
| work in progress at the end of the year | 2 050 |
| closing inventory of finished goods | 2 870 |

What was the cost of production?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Cost of production

  - = prime cost
  - + factory overheads
  - + work in progress at the start of the year
  - - work in progress at the end of the year
- This is the first year of business so there is no work in progress at the start of the year
- Note that the closing inventory of finished goods does not affect the cost of production
- \$65 420 + \$17 270 + \$0 - \$2 050 = \$80 640

**A** is incorrect; the closing inventory of finished goods has also been subtracted

**B** is incorrect;  the closing inventory of finished goods has been subtracted instead of the work in progress at the end of the year

**D** is incorrect; the work in progress at the end of the year has been added not subtracted

parts.problemMd:
A manufacturer’s inventory of raw materials at the start of the year was valued at \$1 500. At the end of the year, it was valued at \$1 250.

What was the effect of this decrease on the cost of production and the cost of sales?

|   | cost of production | cost of sales |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | decrease | decrease |
| **B** | increase | increase |
| **C** | increase | no change |
| **D** | no change | increase |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The cost of raw materials consumed

  - = opening inventory of raw materials
  - + purchases of raw materials
  - - closing inventory of raw materials
- As the opening inventory is bigger than the closing inventory the overall effect is an increase in the cost of raw materials
- Cost of production

  - = prime cost
  
    - this includes the cost of raw materials consumed
  - + factory overheads
  - + work in progress at the start of the year
  - - work in progress at the end of the year
- An increase in the cost of raw materials consumed causes an increase in the cost of production
- Cost of sales

  - = opening inventory of finished goods
  - + cost of production
  - - closing inventory of finished goods
- An increase in the cost of production causes an increase in the cost of sales
- Therefore both the cost of production and the cost of sales increase

**A** is incorrect; this would have been the answer if the closing inventory was greater than the opening inventory

**C** is incorrect; if the cost of production increases then the cost of sales increases

**D** is incorrect; this would have been the answer if the inventories were referring to finished goods rather than raw materials

parts.problemMd:
A manufacturer calculated the cost of production for the year at \$54 500.

It was found that insurance and rates, \$3 400, had been omitted from the financial statements.

Insurance and rates is allocated 80% to the factory and 20% to the offices.

What was the correct cost of production?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The cost of production includes direct costs and indirect costs (factory overheads)

  - costs relating to the offices are not included in the cost of production
  - they will be included as expenses in the income statement
- Calculate the amount of insurance and rates that is allocated to the factory

  - 80% × \$3 400 = \$2 720
- Add this cost to the current cost of production

  - \$54 500 + \$2 720 = \$57 220

**A** is incorrect; the insurance and rates allocated to the factory have been incorrectly subtracted from the current cost of production

**B** is incorrect; the insurance and rates allocated to the offices (instead of those allocated to the factory) have been incorrectly added to the current cost of production

**D** is incorrect; the full amount for insurance and rates has been added to the current cost of production, even though office expenses should not included be in the cost of production

parts.problemMd:
Grace is a sole trader. She is considering forming a partnership with her friend Kelly. What are the disadvantages to Grace of forming a partnership with Kelly?

4. The responsibility for running the business would be shared between Grace and Kelly.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Determine whether each statement is an advantage or disadvantage

  - 1 is a disadvantage as Grace would get less profit
  - 2 is an advantage as there would be more skills in the business
  - 3 is a disadvantage as Kelly would be able to take money from the business which decreases the capital
  - 4 is an advantage as Grace is not solely responsible if the business runs into trouble
  - 1 and 3 are the only disadvantages

**A** is incorrect; it is missing one of the disadvantages

**C** and **D** are incorrect; they contain at least one advantage

parts.problemMd:
What is included in an appropriation account of a partnership?

1. the closing balance on each partner's current account
2. the interest on each partner's capital
3. each partner's share of the residual profit
4. the salary given to each partner
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Determine whether each item appears on the appropriation account

  - 1 is not included in the appropriation account
  - 2 is included in the appropriation account
  - 3 is included in the appropriation account
  - 4 is included in the appropriation account
- 2, 3 and 4 are included in the appropriation account

**A** is incorrect; the closing balance on each partner's current account appears on the statement of financial position

parts.problemMd:
Which items are subtracted from the profit for the year in a partnership appropriation account?

1. interest on drawings
2. interest on capital
3. partners' salaries
4. partners' drawings
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Determine how each item affects the profit for the year

  - 1 is added to the profit for the year
  - 2 is subtracted from the profit for the year
  - 3 is subtracted from the profit for the year
  - 4 does not affect the profit for the year
- 2 and 3 are the only items which are subtracted from the profit for the year

**B** is incorrect; interest on drawings is added to the profit for the year because the business is  owed more money

**C** is incorrect; drawings do not affect the profit for the year

parts.problemMd: Which item appears on the income statement for a partnership?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Interest on loans from partners is a finance cost

  - These are subtracted from the operating profit to find the profit for the year

**B**, **C** and **D** are incorrect; they appear in the appropriation account

parts.problemMd:
How is interest on capital recorded in the books of a partnership?

|   | debit | credit |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | appropriation account | partner's capital account |
| **B** | appropriation account | partner's current account |
| **C** | partner's capital account | appropriation account |
| **D** | partner's current account | appropriation account |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- No entries are made in the partner's capital account unless there is a permanent change to the amount of capital invested

  - Options A and C can be ruled out
- Interest on the partner's capital means the business owes the partner more money

  - Therefore this is a credit entry to the partner's current account
- The interest on capital is also recorded in the appropriation account and it must be a debit to balance the other entry

**A** and **C** are incorrect; interest on capital affects the partner's current account, not the capital account

**D** is incorrect; the partner's current account is debited when the business owes the partner less (for example, when they take drawings)

parts.problemMd:
A partner makes drawings during a financial year.

How is this recorded in the partner’s accounts?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Only entries that affect the permanent capital invested are entered into the partner's capital account

  - This rules out A and C
- Drawings reduce the amount that the business owes the partner

  - Therefore this is a debit entry
- If a partner takes drawings then debit the partner's current account

**A** and **C** are incorrect; drawings do not affect the partner's capital account

**B** is incorrect; credit entries in the partner's current account increase how much is owed to the partner by the business (drawings decrease how much is owed)

parts.problemMd:
Xin and Yuqing are in a partnership. They each maintain both current and capital accounts. An inexperienced book-keeper prepared the following account which contains errors.

Xin capital account

|   | \$ |   | \$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| interest on capital | 2 500 | balance b/d | 50 000 |
| balance c/d | 72 500 | loan made to partnership | 20 000 |
|   | <u>            </u> | drawings | <u>5 000</u> |
|   | <u>75 000</u> |   | <u>75 000</u> |

What should appear as the closing balance on Xin's capital account?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The capital account of each partner is only used for recording the partner's capital contribution and partner's withdrawal of capital

  - Withdrawal of capital is different to taking drawings
  - Drawings are not entered into the capital account
- Drawings and interest on capital are entered into Xin's current account
- A loan made from Xin to the partnership will be entered into a loan account

  - It is not entered in either the capital or the current accounts
- Therefore there have been no transactions that changed the balance on Xin's capital account

  - It remains at \$50 000

**A** is incorrect; you get this answer if you debit the drawings to the capital account (these should be debited to the current account)

**B** is incorrect; you get this answer if you debit the drawings and credit the interest on capital to the capital account (these should be entered into the current account)

**D** is incorrect; you get this answer if you credit the loan to the capital account (this should be credited to a loan account)

parts.problemMd:
Elena and Alessandro are in partnership. The following information relates to Alessandro for the financial year.

|---|---|
| salary | 5 000 |
| drawings | 3 200 |
| share of profit | 8 500 |

The opening credit balance on Alessandro's current account was \$31 400.

What was the closing balance on his current account?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The current account represents how much the business owes each partner
- Salaries and profit shares increase the credit balance

  - The business owes the partner more
- Drawings decrease the credit balance

  - The partner is taking money from the business
  - Therefore, the business owes the partner less
- Add the salary and share of the profit to the opening credit balance

  - \$31 400 + \$5 000 + \$8 500 = \$44 900
- Subtract the drawings

  - \$44 900 - \$3 200 = \$41 700

**A** is incorrect; you get this answer if you forget to include the salary

**C** is incorrect; you get this answer if you forget to include the drawings

**D** is incorrect; you get this answer if you add the drawings instead of subtracting them

parts.problemMd:
Dan and Roger were in a partnership, sharing profits and losses equally. The residual profit for the year, after appropriation, was \$64 000. Roger provided the following information.

|---|---|
| salary | 4 000 |
| drawings | 15 000 |
| interest on capital | 2 000 |
| interest on drawings | 750 |

At the start of the year, Roger's current account had a credit balance of \$2 800.

What was Roger's current account balance at the end of the year?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Share the residual profit equally between the partners

  - \$64 000 ÷ 2 = \$32 000
- Find the total of the credit entries to Roger's current account

  - Interest on capital + salary + profit share
  - \$2 000 + \$4 000 + \$32 000 = \$38 000
- Find the total of the debit entries to Roger's current account

  - Drawings + interest on drawings
  - \$15 000 + \$750 = \$15 750
- Find the new balance

  - Starting balance + credit entries - debit entries
  - \$2 800 + \$38 000 - \$15 750 = \$25 050
  - This is a credit balance because it is a positive value
- Here is how the account will look

| Details | \$ | Details | \$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| drawings | 15 000 | balance b/d | 2 800 |
| interest on drawings | 750 | profit share | 32 000 |
| balance c/d | 25 050 | interest on capital | 2 000 |
|   | <u>               </u> | salary | 4 000 |
|   | <u>40 800</u> |   | <u>40 800</u> |
|   |   | balance b/d | 25 050 |

**A** is incorrect; this is the result if the salary was debited instead of credited

**B** is incorrect; the salary has not been included

| interest on drawings | JP | 500 |   |
|   | Duncan | <u>750</u> | 1 250 |
| salary | Duncan |   | 5 000 |

How much was available for distribution to the partners?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- To calculate the residual profit/loss

  - start with the profit for the year
  - subtract the interest on capital
  
    - this money the business owes to the partners
  - add the interest on drawings
  
    - this money the partners owe to the business
  - subtract the partner's salary
  
    - this money the business owes to the partner
- \$41 500 - \$3 500 + \$1 250 - \$5 000 = \$34 250

**A** is incorrect; you get this value if you subtract the interest on drawings instead of adding it

**C** is incorrect; you get this value if you subtract the interest on drawings and add the interest on capital (it should be the other way around)

**D** is incorrect; you get this value if you forget to subtract the salary

parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Calculate the residual profit

  - Residual profit = profit for the year + interest on drawings - interest on capital - partner's salary
  - \$24 000 + \$600 - \$1 200 - \$1 000 = \$22 400
- Share the residual profit between the partners in the ratio 3 : 4 : 1

parts.problemMd:
Aziz and Bilal are in a partnership with capital of \$30 000 and \$20 000 respectively.

The profit for the year was \$47 000. Neither partner took any drawings during the year.

The partnership agreement provides that profits are to be shared in the proportion to capital invested and each partner is entitled to 5% interest in capital. In addition, Bilal is entitled to an annual salary of \$4 500.

What was the **total **amount credited to Bilal's current account at the end of the year?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Calculate the interest on capital for each partner

  - Aziz: 5% ✕ \$30 000 = \$1 500
  - Bilal: 5% ✕ \$20 000 = \$1 000
  - Total: \$1 500 + \$1 000 = \$2 500
- Calculate the residual profit

  - Residual profit = profit for the year + interest on drawings - interest on capital - partner's salary
  - \$47 000 + \$0 - \$2 500 - \$4 500 = \$40 000
- Share the residual profit between the partners in the given ratio

  - 30 000 : 20 000 is the same as 3 : 2
  - Divide the residual profit by the total number of parts
  
    - \$40 000 ÷ 5 = \$8 000
  - Multiply this by Bilal's part of the ratio
  
    - Bilal: \$8 000 ✕ 2 = \$16 000
- Find the total credit entry to Bilal's current account

  - Interest on capital + salary + profit share
  - \$1 000 + \$4 500 + \$16 000 = \$21 500

**A** is incorrect; this is just Bilal's share of the profits

**C** is incorrect; the \$47 000 has been treated as the residual profit not the profit for the year

**D** is incorrect; this is the total amount credited to Aziz's current account

parts.problemMd:
Ash and Misty are in partnership sharing profits and losses in the ratio of 3 : 1. Ash is entitled to an annual salary of \$6 000. The profit for the year ended 31 March 2024 was \$2 400.

On 1 April 2023, Ash’s current account had a debit balance of \$1 200.

What was the balance on Ash’s current account on 1 April 2024?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A** - Note that the question does not give any information about drawings, interest on drawings or interest on capital - Therefore you should assume that no drawings were taken during the year and that the partnership agreement does not allow interest on capital - Calculate the residual profit - Residual profit = profit for the year + interest on drawings - interest on capital - partner's salary - \$2 400 + \$0 - \$0 - \$6 000 = -\$3 600 - It is a negative therefore it is a loss - Find Ash's share of the loss by dividing the profit into the ratio - \$3 600 ÷ 4 = \$900 - \$900 × 3 = \$2 700 - Find the total of the credit entries in Ash's current account - Interest on capital + salary - \$0 + \$6 000 = \$6 000 - Find the total of the debit entries in Ash's current account - Opening balance + drawings + interest on drawings + share of loss - \$1 200 + \$0 + \$0 + \$2 700 = \$3 900 - The credit total is greater than the debit total so the balance brought down on 1 April will be a credit - Find the balance by finding the difference between the total credits and the total debits - \$6 000 - \$3 900 = \$2 100 - Here is how the account will look | Date | Details | \$ | Date | Details | \$ | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | 2023

March 31 | salary | 6 000 | | 2024

parts.problemMd:
Ishizu and Marik are in a partnership with capital of \$12 000 and \$8 000 respectively.

The **loss **for the year was \$8 500. Only Marik took drawings during the year, these amounted to \$2 000.

The partnership agreement provides that:

- profits and losses are to be shared in the same proportion as the capital invested,
- each partner is entitled to 5% interest on capital,
- each partner is charged 5% on any drawings,
- Marik is entitled to an annual salary of \$800.

What was Marik's share of the residual loss?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- Calculate the interest on capital for each partner

  - Ishizu: 5% × \$12 000 = \$600
  - Marik: 5% × \$8 000 = \$400
  - Total: \$600 + \$400 = \$1 000
- Calculate the interest on drawings

  - Marik: 5% × \$2 000 = \$100
- Calculate the residual profit/loss

  - The business made a loss for the year so treat this as a negative number
  - Residual profit/loss = profit for the year + interest on drawings - interest on capital - partner's salary
  - -\$8 500 + \$100 - \$1 000 - \$800 = -\$10 200
  - This is negative so there was a residual loss not a profit
- Find Marik's share of the loss

  - Divide by the total capital invested
  
    - Total invested = \$12 000 + \$8 000 = \$20 000
    - \$10 200 ÷ \$20 000 = 0.51
  - Multiply by the capital invested by Marik
  
    - 0.51 × \$8 000 = \$4 080

**A** is incorrect; you get this answer if you treat the loss as a positive number instead of a negative number

**C** is incorrect; you get this answer if you subtract the interest on drawings instead of adding it

**D** is incorrect; you get this answer if you subtract the drawings as part of the appropriation of the loss

  - Therefore, the profit will increase by \$1 000

- However, taking goods for the owner's use is a form of drawings

  - This decreases the capital by \$1 000

  - This is because they were still due during the financial period

- Subtract the \$150 prepaid expense from the expenses amount on the income statement

  - This is because they were due in the following financial period not the period relating to the income statement
  - Therefore the expenses decrease by \$150
- Profit = gross profit + other income - expenses

  - If the expenses increase by \$500 then the profit decreases by \$500
  - If the expenses decrease by \$150 then the profit increases by \$150
- Correct profit = \$18 400 - \$500 + \$150 = \$18 050

  - 100% + 20% = 120%

- You can find the cost of sales by multiplying the average inventory by the rate of inventory turnover

**A** is incorrect; you get this value if you reverse the inventories (add the opening and subtract the closing)

| opening inventory | 9 000 |
| purchases | 121 000 |
| closing inventory | 15 000 |

What was the rate of inventory turnover?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Calculate the cost of sales

  - Opening inventory + Purchases - Closing inventory
  - \$9 000 + \$121 000 - \$15 000 = \$115 000
- Calculate the average inventory

  - $\frac{\mathrm{Opening} \mathrm{inventory}+\mathrm{Closing} \mathrm{inventory}}{2}$
  - $\frac{\$ 9 000 + \$ 15 000}{2} = \$ 12 000$
- Calculate the rate of inventory turnover

  - $\frac{\mathrm{Cost} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{sales}}{\mathrm{Average} \mathrm{inventory}}$
  - $\frac{115000}{12000}=9.58333...$
- Round to two decimal places

  - Rate of inventory turnover = 9.58 times

**A** is incorrect; this is what you would get if you used \$24 000 for the average inventory (instead of dividing by 2 to get \$12 000)

**B** is incorrect; this is what you would get if you used \$130 000 for the cost of sales (instead of subtracting the closing inventory to get \$115 000), and if you used \$24 000 for the average inventory (instead of dividing by 2 to get \$12 000)

**D** is incorrect; this is what you would get if you used \$130 000 for the cost of sales (instead of subtracting the closing inventory to get \$115 000)

**A** is incorrect; the gross margin represents the proportion of the revenue that is turned into gross profit

**B** is incorrect; the profit margin represents the proportion of the revenue that is turned into profit for the year

parts.problemMd: Which one of the following is **not** a limitation of inter-firm comparison?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Consider the options given
- Option A

  - Businesses only report on financial information
  
    - So comparisons cannot be made about employees' satisfaction, skills, experience, etc.
  - This **is** a limitation of inter-firm comparison
- Option B

  - Comparisons should be made between businesses which are roughly the same age
  
    - Newer businesses are likely to have higher expenses and liabilities
    - More experienced businesses are likely to have developed a loyal customer base and a good reputation
  - This **is** a limitation of inter-firm comparison
- Option C

  - This is **not** a limitation of inter-firm comparison
  
    - Different businesses may set different sales prices
    - But the effects of this on profitability and other measures of success will be contained in the accounting records
- Option D

  - Businesses might have different financial periods
  
    - The end date of a financial year can impact the financial position of the business
    
      - E.g., inventory levels can be affected by the seasons and holidays
  - This **is** a limitation of inter-firm comparison

**A**, **B** and **D** are incorrect; each of these *is* a limitation of inter-firm comparison

parts.problemMd:
The following is the list of balances for a company at 31 August 2024.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| cash in hand | 375 |
| bank loan - repayable 30 November 2024 | 2 500 |
| bank loan - repayable 31 January 2026 | 4 000 |
| bank overdraft | 250 |
| trade receivables | 9 200 |
| trade payables | 5 800 |
| other receivables | 300 |
| other payables | 105 |
| inventory | 21 000 |

What was the current ratio?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Calculate the total current assets

  - Cash in hand + Trade receivables + Other receivables + Inventory
  - \$375 + \$9 200 + \$300 + \$21 000 = \$30 875
- Calculate the total current liabilities

  - Bank loan (repayable 30 Nov 2024) + Bank overdraft + Trade payables + Other payables
  - \$2 500 + \$250 + \$5 800 + \$105 = \$8 655
- Be careful - the bank loan (repayable 31 Jan 2026) is *not* a current liability because it is not due within a year
- Calculate the current ratio

  - $\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets}}{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{liabilities}}$
  - $\frac{30875}{8655}=3.567302...$
- Round to two decimal places and write as a ratio

  - Current ratio = 3.57 : 1

**A** is incorrect; this is the answer you would get if inventory was left out of the current assets

**B** is incorrect; this is the answer you would get if you included the non-current bank loan in the current liabilities

**D** is incorrect; this is the answer you would get if you didn't include either of the bank loans in the current liabilities

parts.problemMd: Which of the following changes might a business make in order to reduce its liquid (acid test) ratio?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Liquid (acid test) ratio is $\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets}-\mathrm{Inventory}}{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{liabilities}}$
- That ratio can be reduced by

  - reducing current assets
  - increasing inventory
  - increasing current liabilities
- Reducing trade receivables reduces current assets

  - So the correct answer is D

**A** is incorrect; reducing bank overdraft reduces current liabilities, which will tend to increase the liquid (acid test) ratio

**B** is incorrect; reducing inventory will tend to increase the liquid (acid test) ratio

**C** is incorrect; reducing other payables reduces current liabilities, which will tend to increase the liquid (acid test) ratio

parts.problemMd:
The following table contains accounting ratios relating to the businesses owned by Awinita and Tokala.

|   | Awinita | Tokala |
|---|---|---|
| liquid (acid test) ratio | 1.2 : 1 | 0.9 : 1 |
| current ratio | 2.1 : 1 | 2.5 : 1 |

Which of the following statements are correct?

1    Awinita has insufficient current assets to meet her current liabilities.

2   Awinita can meet her current liabilities from her liquid assets more easily than Tokala.

3   Tokala has sufficient liquid assets to meet his current liabilities.

4   Tokala can meet his current liabilities from his current assets more easily than Awinita.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- Liquid (acid test) ratio is represents the amount of liquid assets (cash and receivables) available to cover each \$1 of current liability

  - If it is above 1:1 then the business has enough liquid assets to cover its short-term debts (even if the inventory cannot be sold)
- Current ratio represents the amount of current assets available to cover  each \$1 of current liability

  - If it is above 1:1 then the business has enough current assets (including inventory) to cover its short-term debts
- Of the 4 statements:

  - (1) is incorrect
  
    - Awinita's current ratio (2.1 : 1) says that she has \$2.10 in current assets for every \$1 of current liability, so she has sufficient current assets to meet her current liabilities
  - (2) is correct
  
    - Awinita's liquid ratio (1.2 : 1) is higher than Tokala's (0.9 : 1), so she can more easily meet her current liabilities from liquid assets
  - (3) is incorrect
  
    - Tokala's liquid ratio (0.9 : 1) says that he only has \$0.90 in liquid assets for every \$1 of current liability, so he has insufficient liquid assets to meet his current liabilities
  - (4) is correct
  
    - Tokala's current ratio (2.5 : 1) is higher than Awinita's (2.1 : 1), so he can more easily meet his current liabilities from current assets
- So '2 and 4' (choice C) is the correct answer

**A**, **B** and** D** are incorrect because they each contain one correct and one incorrect statement from the list of four statements

parts.problemMd:
Arvan took out a long-term bank loan and used some of the funds to to pay some of his credit suppliers early.

How did this affect his business's return on capital employed (ROCE) and trade payables turnover (days)?

|   | return on capital employed (ROCE) | trade payables turnover (days) |
|---|---|---|
| **A** | decrease | decrease |
| **B** | decrease | increase |
| **C** | increase | decrease |
| **D** | increase | increase |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct solution is A**

- Consider the ROCE formula
$\frac{\mathrm{Operating} \mathrm{profit} \mathrm{for} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{year}}{\mathrm{Capital} \mathrm{employed}}\times100$

  - Operating profit for the year does not have loan interest subtracted
  
    - So the long-term loan doesn't change the operating profit
  - Capital employed = Equity (or capital) + Non-current liabilities
  
    - The long-term loan increases non-current liabilities
    - So it increases capital employed
  - The top of the fraction in the ROCE formula stays the same
  
    - And the bottom increases
    - So ROCE decreases
- Consider the trade payables turnover formula
$\frac{\mathrm{Trade} \mathrm{payables}}{\mathrm{Credit} \mathrm{purchases}}\times365$

  - Using the loan to pay credit suppliers decreases trade payables
  - The long-term loan does not affect credit purchases
  - The top of the fraction in the trade payables turnover formula decreases
  
    - And the bottom stays the same
    - So trade payables turnover decreases

**B **is incorrect; trade payables turnover is decreased

**C** is incorrect; ROCE is decreased

**D** is incorrect; both accounting ratios are decreased

- The formula for trade receivables turnover is

  - $\frac{\mathrm{Trade} \mathrm{receivables}}{\mathrm{Credit} \mathrm{sales}}\times365$
  - The answer is a number of days, and should always be rounded up to the next whole day
- Using the numbers from Madison's information

  - $\frac{20480}{267000}\times365=27.997...$
  - That rounds up to 28 days

**A** is incorrect; you would get this answer if you divided the trade receivables by the sum of cash and credit sales

**B** is incorrect; you would get this answer if you divided the sum of trade and other receivables by the sum of cash and credit sales

**D** is incorrect; you would get this answer if you divided the sum of trade and other receivables by credit sales

parts.problemMd:
Hypatia owns and operates a bookshop. Which actions could she take to improve her rate of inventory turnover?

1. increase the selling price of all her books
2. offer discounts on books over a year old
3. pay her book suppliers as quickly as possible
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The rate of inventory turnover formula is $\frac{\mathrm{Cost} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{sales}}{\mathrm{Average} \mathrm{inventory}}$

  - This can be improved by
  
    - increasing the volume of sales
    - reducing the amount of inventory that is held by the business
- Consider the 3 actions

  - Action 1
  
    - Increasing the selling price of her books is likely to *decrease* the volume of sales
    - This will not improve the rate of inventory turnover
  - Action 2
  
    - Offering discounts on books over a year old is likely to increase the volume of sales
    
      - and by reducing older stock is also likely to reduce the amount of inventory held
    - This will improve the rate of inventory turnover
  - Action 3
  
    - Paying her suppliers quickly will not affect volume of sales or the amount of inventory held by the business
    - This will not improve the rate of inventory turnover
- So 2 is the only one of the three actions that might improve Hypatia's rate of inventory turnover

**A** and **B** are incorrect; 1 and 3 will not improve her rate of inventory turnover

**D** is incorrect; 3 will not improve her rate of inventory turnover

parts.problemMd:
A trader provided the following information for the year ended 31 December.

|   | \$ |
|---|---|
| total cash and credit purchases of goods for resale | 240 000 |
| cash purchases of goods for resale | 23 000 |
| credit purchases of non-current assets | 35 000 |

Her trade payables at that date were \$16 000.

What was the trade payables turnover?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The formula for trade payables turnover is

  - $\frac{\mathrm{Trade} \mathrm{payables}}{\mathrm{Credit} \mathrm{purchases}}\times365$
- Trade payables are \$16 000
- To find credit purchases, subtract 'cash purchases of goods for resale' from 'total cash and credit purchases of goods for resale'

  - \$240 000 - \$23 000 = \$217 000
- Put those numbers into the formula

  - $\frac{16000}{217000}\times365=26.912...$
  - That rounds up to 27 days

**A** is incorrect;  you would get this if you divided by the sum of total cash and credit purchases of goods for resale and credit purchases of non-current assets

**B** is incorrect;  you would get this if you divided by the total cash and credit purchases of goods for resale

**D** is incorrect;  you would get this if you divided by the difference of total cash and credit purchases of goods for resale and credit purchases of non-current assets

parts.problemMd:
Aryana, a sole trader, provides the following information for her business.

| credit sales | \$48 000 |
|---|---|
| cash sales | 20% of total sales |
| net profit margin | 25% |

How much is the net profit?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Net profit margin is $\frac{\mathrm{Net} \mathrm{profit}}{\mathrm{Revenue}}\times100$

  - Here you want to find the net profit
  
    - You can do this by finding the 'net profit margin %' of the revenue
    - So here the net profit will be 25% of the revenue
- The revenue is credit sales + cash sales
- You are told the credit sales (\$48 000)
- Cash sales are 20% of total sales

  - That means that credit sales are 100-20=80% of total sales
  - So 80% of total sales = \$48 000
  - That means 10% of total sales = $\frac{\$ 48 000}{8}$=\$6 000
  - And 20% of total sales is $\$ 6 000 \times 2$ = \$12 000
  - So cash sales = \$12 000
- Revenue = credit sales + cash sales = \$48 000 + \$12 000 = \$60 000
- Therefore net profit = 25% of \$60 000 = \$15 000

**A** is incorrect; this is what you would get if you reduced the credit sales by 20% (to \$38 400) and then found 25% of that

**B** is incorrect; this is what you would get if you ignored the cash sales and just found 25% of \$48 000

**C** is incorrect; this is what you would get if you calculated the cash sales as \$9 600 (20% of \$48 000)

parts.problemMd:
A business provides the following information.

| liquid (acid test) ratio | 2.2 : 1 |
|---|---|
| current liabilities | \$15 000 |
| inventory | \$8 000 |

What is the value of the current assets?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The liquid (acid test) ratio is $\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets}-\mathrm{Inventory}}{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{liabilities}}$

  - Here that is equal to 2.2
  - Inventory = \$8 000
  - Current liabilities = \$15 000
- Put all that info into an equation

  - $\frac{\mathrm{Current} \mathrm{assets}-8000}{15000}=2.2$
- Multiply both sides by 15 000 (i.e. multiply the 15 000 across the equation)

  - This gets rid of the fraction
  - $\begin{gathered} \text{Current} \text{assets} - 8 000 & = 2.2 \times 15000 \\ \text{Current} \text{assets} - 8 000 & = 33 000 \end{gathered}$
- Add 8 000 to both sides (i.e. the -8 000 on the left-hand side becomes a +8 000 on the right)

  - $\begin{array}{ccc}Current \text{assets} & = & 33 000 + 8 000 \\ Current \text{assets} & = & 41 000\end{array}$

**A** is incorrect; this is what you would get if you multiplied the inventory (\$8 000) by 2.2

**B** is incorrect; this is what you would get if you subtracted \$8 000 from \$33 000 instead of adding it

**C** is incorrect; this is what you would get if you multiplied the current liabilities (\$15 000) by 2.2, but didn't then add on \$8 000 for the inventory

% | profit margin

- The difference** **between the gross margin and profit margin is the proportion** **of revenue that is spent on overheads (i.e. expenses)** **after deducting other income

  - A smaller difference indicates that a business has better control of overheads
- Calculate the difference for each of the businesses

  - Bidziil: 36-17=19
  - Chayton: 34-16=18
  - Doli: 31-11=20
- Chayton's business has the smallest difference, so that is the business that most efficiently controls its overheads

**A**, **B** and** D** are incorrect; the difference for each of those businesses is higher than the one for the correct answer

|   | \$ |

| equity at the year-end | 210 000 |
| 6% debentures | 35 000 |

What was WWL Limited's return on capital employed?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The return on capital employed is $\frac{\mathrm{Operating} \mathrm{profit} \mathrm{for} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{year}}{\mathrm{Capital} \mathrm{employed}}\times100$
- The operating profit for the year here is the 'net profit before interest' (\$43 100)
- Capital employed = Equity + Non-current liabilities

  - Debenture debt is a non-current liability, so
  - Capital employed = 210 000 + 35 000 = 245 000
- ROCE = $\frac{43100}{245000}\times100$ = 17.591836...

parts.problemMd:
Yakub made credit sales of \$120 450 in each of the years 2022 and 2023.

In 2023, his trade receivables turnover was exactly three days longer than it had been in 2022.

What was the **change** in his total trade receivables in 2023?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- Start with the formula for trade receivables turnover

  - $\frac{\mathrm{Trade} \mathrm{receivables}}{\mathrm{Credit} \mathrm{sales}}\times365$
  - That gives the number of days
- Credit sales is the same for both years

  - So the only difference is in the trade receivables
- If the turnover was longer in 2023 than it was in 2022

  - then the trade receivables must have been greater in 2023 than in 2022
  - This rules out answers A and C
  - At this point you would have a 50% chance of guessing correctly between B and D
  
    - even if you couldn't work out the rest of the answer!
- To work out the amount, first write the 2022 and 2023 trade receivables turnovers, filling in the numbers you know

  - 2022: $\frac{\mathrm{TR}_{2022}}{120450}\times365$
  - 2023: $\frac{\mathrm{TR}_{2023}}{120450}\times365$
  - $\mathrm{TR}_{2022}$ and $\mathrm{TR}_{2023}$ stand for 'Trade Receivables 2022' and 'Trade Receivables 2023', respectively
- We know that the turnover was three days longer in 2023 than in 2022

  - That means that
  
    - $( \frac{TR_{2023} }{120 450} \times 365 ) - ( \frac{TR_{2022} }{120 450} \times 365 ) = 3$
  - Multiply both sides by 120 450 (i.e., 'multiply the 120 450 across')
  
    - $( TR_{2023} \times 365 ) - ( TR_{2022} \times 365 ) = 361 350$
  - Dividing both sides by 365
  
    - $\mathrm{TR}_{2023}-\mathrm{TR}_{2022}=990$
  - Therefore
  
    - $\mathrm{TR}_{2023}=\mathrm{TR}_{2022}+990$
  - So total trade receivables in 2023 showed a \$990 increase over 2022
- Alternatively, divide the credit sales by 365 days to find the average sales each day

  - \$120 450 ÷ 365 days = \$330 per day
- Multiply this by the 3 extra days

  - \$330 × 3 = \$990

**A** and **B** are incorrect; you might find 110 for the amount if you divided 120 450 by 365 (=330), and then divided that by the number of days difference (330 ÷ 3 = 110)

**C** is incorrect; the amount is correct, but it is given as a decrease instead of an increase

parts.problemMd:
Azaf, a trader, records assets in his ledger using the price he paid for them.

Which accounting principle is he applying?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- The accounting principle of historic cost states:

  - Assets and liabilities are valued at the cost of the original transaction and kept as such on the financial statements

**A** is incorrect; prudence states that a business should not overstate its profit or its net assets

**B** is incorrect; materiality states that transactions which have a low monetary value can be grouped rather than entered into separate accounts

**C** is incorrect; matching states that incomes and expenses must be matched to the year to which they relate or in which the benefit is gained

parts.problemMd:
A restaurant owner made no entry in her accounts when the business received a good rating from a customer.

Which accounting principle was applied?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The accounting principle of money measurement states:

  - Financial statements only contain information about the transactions involving money
- Customer ratings do not involve money

**B** is incorrect; historic cost states that assets and liabilities are valued at the cost of the original transaction and kept as such on the financial statements

**C** is incorrect; going concern states that it is assumed that a business will continue to operate into the foreseeable future by undertaking its current trading activities

**D** is incorrect; realisation states that business transactions are only recorded in the financial statements when a payment is made or the ownership has been transferred

parts.problemMd:
Azaf is an accountant. When he prepares financial statements he makes sure that they are clearly presented and he assumes that the users of these statements will have a reasonable knowledge of accounting.

Which accounting policy is Azaf is applying?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- For the financial statements to meet the understandability policy:

  - the accounting information provided should be clear so that users can easily understand it
  - It can be assumed that the users have a reasonable understanding of accounting terms

**A** is incorrect; comparability refers to the ability to use the financial statements to compare one set with another set from a previous year or another business

**B** is incorrect; relevance refers to producing the statements promptly so that the information is still useful and helpful for decision-making

**C** is incorrect; reliability refers to producing financial statements which are free from errors and bias

parts.problemMd: Which accounting policy requires that the information in financial statements is useful for making financial decisions for the future?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The relevance policy requires that:

  - the accounting information should be provided in a timely manner so that it is relevant to the users
  - financial decisions affecting the future of the business should be able to be made from the information

**A** is incorrect; comparability refers to the ability to use the financial statements to compare one set with another set from a previous year or another business

**B** is incorrect; this is an accounting principle not policy

**D** is incorrect; reliability refers to producing financial statements which are free from errors and bias

parts.problemMd:
Jamie is the owner of a business.

Jack opens up a rival business in the same town as Jamie. Jamie knows that this will affect his sales but did not record this in his accounting records.

Which accounting principle is Jamie applying?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The accounting principle of money measurement states:

  - financial statements only contain information about the transactions involving money

**A** is incorrect; consistency refers to applying the same accounting procedures each year (such as depreciation)

**B** is incorrect; duality refers to transactions being entered into the books twice on opposite sides

**D** is incorrect; prudence states that the profit and the valuation of assets should not be overstated

parts.problemMd:
Each year, Mariam uses the reducing balance method to depreciate her vehicles.

Which accounting principle is Mariam observing?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- The principle of consistency states:

  - when a business chooses a method for a particular item, it should continue to use that method each year

**B** is incorrect; duality refers to transactions being entered into the books twice on opposite sides

parts.problemMd:
An ice cream business purchases a cheap calculator during the financial year.

Why would the ice cream business **not **include the value of the calculator in the statement of financial position?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The accounting principle of materiality states:

  - Transactions which have a low monetary value can be grouped rather than entered into separate accounts
- This means that the calculator can be classified as a sundry expense instead of an asset

**A** is incorrect; the business still purchased the calculator regardless of whether it has been used or not

parts.problemMd:
Sofia, a credit customer of a trader, is unable to pay their invoice. The trader decides to write off the balance as an irrecoverable debt.

The trader makes a credit entry in Sofia's account and a debit entry in the irrecoverable debts account.

Which accounting principles are being applied?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The duality principle is being applied

  - A debit entry and a credit entry are being made
- The prudence principle is being applied

  - The debt is being written off so that the value of the assets and/or profit are not overstated

**A** and **C** are incorrect; the realisation principle is not being applied as the amount has already been recorded in Sofia's account

**D** is incorrect; neither principle is being applied

parts.problemMd:

Which accounting principles were being applied?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- The duality principle is being applied

  - A debit entry and a credit entry are being made
- The business entity principle is being applied

  - The car is not being purchased for the business therefore the debit entry is made to the drawings account and not an assets account

**A** is incorrect; the prudence principle does not apply as the value of the assets and the profit are not being overstated

**C** is incorrect; the matching principle does not apply as the transaction does not affect multiple financial periods

**D** is incorrect; neither of the principles are being applied

- The duality principle is being applied

  - A debit entry and a credit entry are being made
- The business entity principle is being applied

  - The money was introduced by the owner so it goes in the capital account rather than a loan account

**B** is incorrect; the going concern principle is not explicitly being applied as the business is just starting up

**C** is incorrect; the materiality principle does not apply as the transaction involves a large amount of money

**D** is incorrect; neither of the principles are being applied

parts.problemMd:
Wasim is a trader. His financial year ends on 31 March.

The totals of his trial balance on 31 March 2017 did not agree. The difference was a shortage on the debit side of \$495. This was entered in a suspense account.

The following errors were later discovered.

1. The total of a page of the purchases account, \$3842, had been carried forward as \$3824.
2. A cheque received from DEC Limited, \$150, had been credited to the account of DDE Limited.
3. The balance of the petty cash book, \$100, had been omitted from the trial balance.
4. Repairs to a motor vehicle, \$283, had been debited to the motor vehicles account.
5. Purchase of fixtures, \$2000, on credit from OS Supplies had been debited to OS Supplies and credited to fixtures account.
6. The total of the discount allowed column in the cash book, \$250, had been credited to the discount received account in the ledger.
7. The total of the analysis column for stationery in the petty cash book, \$67, had not been transferred to the stationery account in the ledger.

**REQUIRED **

Prepare the suspense account. Start with the balance arising from the difference on the trial balance. The account should be balanced or totalled as necessary.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 7 mark in total.
> 
> - 1 mark for the correct details and amount for each of the following.
> 
> **Explanation**
> 
> Go through each error individually and consider the correct entries.
> 
> - Put the difference on trial balance of \$495 on the debit side
> 
>   - This is because the credit total was \$495 more than the debit balance
> - Put an entry of \$18 for purchases on the credit side
> 
>   - **Error 1** is an addition error
>   - The purchases debit balance is undercast by \$18
>   - Fix the error by:
>   
>     - debiting the purchases account
>     - crediting the suspense account
> - Put an entry of \$100 for petty cash on the credit side
> 
>   - **Error 3** is an error of partial omission
>   - The petty cash debit balance has been omitted
>   - Fix the error by:
>   
>     - debiting the petty cash account
>     - crediting the suspense account
> - Put an entry of \$250 for discount received on the credit side
> 
>   - **Error 6** is an error of posting
>   - The discount received account had been credited by mistake
>   - Fix the error by:
>   
>     - debiting the discount received account
>     - crediting the suspense account
> - Put an entry of \$250 for discount allowed on the credit side
> 
>   - **Error 6** is an error of posting
>   - The debit entry has been missed from the discount allowed account
>   - Fix the error by:
>   
>     - debiting the discount allowed  account
>     - crediting the suspense account
> - Put an entry of \$67 for stationery on the credit side
> 
>   - **Error 7** is an error of partial omission
>   - The debit entry has been missed from the stationery account
>   - Fix the error by:
>   
>     - debiting the stationery  account
>     - crediting the suspense account
> - Balance the account and bring down the balance
> 
>   - You get the mark for using your **own figures**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Normally, suspense accounts balance out. However, this one does not. This means there are further undiscovered errors. The question hints at this by saying "The account should be balanced or totalled as necessary".
> 
> Errors 2, 4 and 5 do not affect the trial balance and do not require the suspense account to fix them.
> 
> Error 2 is an error of commission. The total for trade receivables is correct even though the balances for individual accounts are incorrect
> 
> Error 4 is an error of principle. The balance for motor vehicles repairs is under by \$283 and the balance for motor vehicles is over by \$283. Both accounts have debit balances, so the errors balance out.
> 
> Error 5 is an error of complete reversal. The amounts are correct, but the debit and credit entries are the wrong way around.

Complete the table to show the entries required to correct each error. The first one has been completed as an example.

| Error | Entries required to correct the error |   |   |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|

| Eshe’s total drawings from the bank for her own use, \$9500, had been debited to the cash account. |   |   |   |   |
| A purchases invoice from Danika for \$137 had been recorded in her account and in the purchases journal as \$173. |   |   |   |   |

parts.problemMd:
Eshe’s capital at 1 April 2022 was \$31000. Her draft profit for the year ended 31 March 2023 before correction of the errors was \$15600.

**REQUIRED **

Calculate Eshe’s capital at 31 March 2023 **after** the errors have been corrected.
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **\$37 402**

Calculation of closing capital

|   | \$ |   | \$ |   | \$ |   |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Capital at 1 April 2022 |   |   |   |   | 31 000 | **[1]** |
| Draft profit |   |   | 15 600 |   |   |   |
| Add Credit sales to Raymond | 210 | **[1]** |   |   |   |   |
| Purchase from Danika | 36 | **[1]** |   |   |   |   |
| Motor expenses | <u>100</u> | **[1]** | <u>346</u> |   |   |   |
|   |   |   | 15 946 |   |   |   |
| Less Sales returns |   |   | <u>44</u> | **[1]** | <u>15 902</u> |   |
|   |   |   |   |   | 46 902 |   |
| Less Drawings |   |   |   |   | <u>9 500</u> | **[1]** |
|   |   |   |   |   | <u>37 402</u> | **[1]** |

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 7 marks in total.
> 
> **Explanation**
> 
> - 1 mark for adding the draft profit to the opening capital
> - 1 mark **each **for adding the following to the draft profit
> 
>   - Sales invoice to Raymond
>   - Purchases invoice from Danika
>   - Motor expenses
> - 1 mark for subtracting the sales returns from the draft profit
> - 1 mark for subtracting the drawings from the opening capital
> - 1 mark for using your **own figures** to calculate the closing capital
> 
> You do not need to set your answer out like a table. However, it is a logical method and clearly shows your calculation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Remember, the formula to find the closing capital:
> 
> closing capital = opening capital + profit for the year - drawings
> 
> An easy way to determine the effects on the profit is to identify the accounts which relate to expenses or income. Then any credit entries in these account increase profit and any debits decrease the profit.

Find the total depreciation for the vehicle that was sold on 31 December 2024

- Find the yearly depreciation charge

$20 \% \times 12000 = 2400$

- Find the number of years that Roger owned the vehicle

*1 July 2022 to 31 December 2024 = 2.5 years*

$2.5\times2400=6000$

Find the depreciation charge for the year ended 30 June 2025

- The charge for the vehicle sold halfway through the year is

$1 \frac{1}{2} \times 20 \% \times 12000 = 1200$

- The charge for the other vehicles Roger owned at the start of the year is

$20 \% \times ( 85000 - 12000 ) = 14600$

- The charge for the new vehicle purchases at the start of the year is

$20 \% \times 20000 = 4000$

- Add the charges together

$1200+14600+4000=19800$

parts.problemMd:
Nala is planning to expand her business and to take out a bank loan to finance the expansion. The loan would be repayable after five years.

**REQUIRED**

Advise Nala whether she should obtain a bank loan to expand the business. Justify your answer by providing **two **points for and **two **points against obtaining the bank loan to expand the business.
parts.solutionMd:
If Nala obtained a bank loan to expand the business, then her profits might increase **[1]**. And once the loan is paid off, Nala will have no liability to the bank **[1]**.

However, Nala will have to pay the loan back and if she can't then her non-current assets might be at risk **[1]**. Also, she will have to pay interest on the loan, which will reduce the profits **[1]**.

Nala should not obtain a bank loan **[1]** as her profit margin is already low.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 5 marks in total:
> 
> - 1 mark for your **decision**.
> - Maximum 4 marks for **points for **and **points against **obtaining a bank loan to expand the business.
> 
>   - Up to 2 marks for **points for**.
>   - Up to 2 marks for **points against**.
> 
> **Points for **may include:
> 
> - The profit might increase if Nala expands the business
> - Nala will not have any liability to the bank once the loan is paid off
> - Nala has five years to repay the loan
> - Other valid points for are accepted
> 
> **Points against **may include:
> 
> - The loan must be repaid
> - Nala will have to pay interest on the loan
> - Nala would likely need to use the property or other non-current assets as security for the loan
> - The bank might be unwilling to offer a loan
> - Other valid points against are accepted

parts.problemMd:
Ramla has calculated her draft profit figure for the year ended 28 February 2023. Adjustments in Ramla’s ledger accounts have still to be made for the following items

1. An amount of \$99 owed to Ramla by Mai is to be written off as irrecoverable.
2. Drawings, \$120, had been debited to the wages account

Ramla prepares journal entries to correct the errors.

**REQUIRED **

Explain

(i) how the journal for item 1 complies with the prudence principle.

(ii) how the journal for item 2 complies with the business entity principle.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The prudence principle states that a business should not overstate its profits and assets **[1 mark]**

Irrecoverable debts should be written off to ensure the profit is not overstated **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 2 marks in total:
> 
> - 1 mark for explaining the principle.
> - 1 mark for explaining how the item adheres to the principle.
> 
> Other acceptable answers for the first mark  include:
> 
> - The prudence principle states that a business should not understate its losses and liabilities
> 
> Other acceptable answers for the second mark  include:
> 
> - Irrecoverable debts should be written off to ensure the assets are not overstated
> - Irrecoverable debts should be written off to not understate the loss

(ii)

The business entity principle states that a business should be regarded as separate to its owners **[1 mark]**

Drawings are when money is taken from the business by the owner so it should be recorded as drawings not wages to ensure that the profits are not understated **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 2 marks in total:
> 
> - 1 mark for explaining the principle.
> - 1 mark for explaining how the item adheres to the principle.
> 
> Other acceptable answers for the first mark  include:
> 
> - The business entity principle states that transactions should be recorded from the point of view of the business
> 
> Other acceptable answers for the second mark  include:
> 
> - Drawings should be recorded to ensure that the capital is not overstated
